item.title: AI has scraped nearly the entire internet. It still can't touch the one thing that matters…
item.description:
AI has scraped nearly the entire internet. It still can't touch the one thing that matters, and it's sat between your ears.
Here's what keeps me up, and I run an AI content startup so this should be the last thing I'd say.
Every tool works the same way. It scrapes what's already online, except half of online is already AI now.
Slop in, slop out, blander every pass.
A machine writing for machines to scrape. Dead internet, live, and my own industry flooring it.
You can copy the point but not the vector.
You can copy where someone landed. You can't copy the mind that keeps getting them there.
That's the whole reason Draper doesn't just scrape the internet. It scrapes you. The calls, the thing you've said out loud fifty times and never thought to write down.
So what goes back out is actually new. Not more slop on the pile, it's you, amplified.

item.title: One of my front of house guys at Simply Smashed found out about the Goldman bit mid-shift …
item.description:
One of my front of house guys at Simply Smashed found out about the Goldman bit mid-shift and just went "you left Goldman Sachs for this?"
He wasn't taking the piss either. He actually felt sorry for me.
Goldman Sachs, then a social media startup, then a burger shop, then a ghostwriting agency, now an AI content startup.
Everyone gets stuck on the burger bit and it's the least interesting jump on there.
Goldman put me on a team nobody had a plan for, which is how I ended up in a prayer room asking a guy about the janky donation app he'd coded himself, and then working on it.
There were four of us. I did users and support, worked out what we should build next, and posted about all of it on Twitter. One of those posts went viral during Ramadan and thousands of people ended up donating pennies through it.
Then Simply Smashed.
We set the dark kitchen up, then I left to study in Egypt for nine months while my brother and my dad kept it running.
I came back and my brother gave me one rule. Your job is to grow it.
And there were long stretches in there where I thought the front of house guy had a point.
When you're inside it every day you can't tell whether any of it is working, and I'd catch myself wondering if I should have stayed in tech.
We had nothing to spend so I used what I already knew worked, got into how the kitchen ran and what we were putting out, and told the story publicly the whole way through.
It ended up the highest rated burger joint in London.
Which got me in the door at the agency, where I trained the writers and worked out that the instinct I'd been running on since I was 19 was an entire industry. One that AI was about to turn over completely.
I didn't fancy watching that happen from inside someone else's company.
So, Draper.
I don't think I ever actually answered him.

item.title: I've written for founders inside YC and a16z portfolio companies. Over 20 million views in…
item.description:
I've written for founders inside YC and a16z portfolio companies. Over 20 million views in two years.
Almost none of it came from a new story.
It came from about five, told properly, from a different side each time.
Almost everyone thinks that's cheating.
Half of everything your LinkedIn post will ever do happens in the first 23 hours.
Scott Graffius ran the numbers on 5.6 million posts across eleven platforms. He measured how long each one takes to pick up half the engagement it will ever get.
A LinkedIn post: 23 hours. A blog post: just over two years.
Which makes a blog post outlive a LinkedIn post by 767 times.
(TikTok and Snapchat both came out at zero minutes, which feels about right.)
So founders sit on their best story for weeks. Waiting for the right moment to tell it properly.
Then they tell it once, watch it die by Thursday, and never go near it again. Because using it twice feels like cheating.
Every writer you actually rate is doing the same thing. It's a busy feed. Almost nobody saw it the first time and the ones who did have forgotten.
I did it to you last week. Tuesday and Thursday, both about the same year at Goldman when I was 18. One was the side project I talked my way onto. One was the rooms I had no business sitting in.
The version doing the rounds is take one belief and chop it into a week of posts. It's what every repurposing tool on the market spits out. Paste in the post, get ten variations back, schedule the lot.
You can spot it instantly. The first one's alright. The rest are the same sentence with the paragraphs moved around.
A belief doesn't have a week of posts in it. A morning where the whole thing nearly fell over does.
You can come at that morning from what it cost you. Or from what the person across the table actually said. Or from the bit you got wrong and didn't admit to anyone for another year.
So we go back to the morning and find the angle we didn't use the first time.
Nobody has ever mentioned it once.

item.title: I was 18 and got placed on the wrong team at Goldman Sachs. They'd just launched a technol…
item.description:
I was 18 and got placed on the wrong team at Goldman Sachs.
They'd just launched a technology apprenticeship, first cohort ever, and I was supposed to go into a traditional software engineering role but instead I ended up on something called the voice engineering team where the second youngest person was at least double my age.
So I just started showing up to things.
That's how I ended up sat in rooms watching Amazon and Cisco pitch Goldman on replacing the hoots and the turrets... the hoots are the broadcast intercoms and the turrets are these massive phone setups bolted to every trader's desk. Multimillion pound infrastructure decisions and I'm there acting like I belong.
I'm watching pitches fall apart, watching projects get greenlit and then quietly die six months later, and I'm realising the interesting stuff isn't just the engineering it's everything around it.
I moved into a proper engineering role eventually.
But I think about that stretch a lot because nobody was checking on me, no one would've noticed if I'd just sat at my desk and coasted through it. It would've been the easiest thing in the world to do nothing.
I just kept walking into rooms I had no business being in because I wanted to know what was going on.

item.title: I got 6 A*s and 5 As at GCSE. Then I got BBDD at A-level. Nobody's mentioned the GCSEs sin…
item.description:
I got 6 A*s and 5 As at GCSE.
Then I got BBDD at A-level.
Nobody's mentioned the GCSEs since. But I still hear about the A-levels.
At 16 I was coasting and I didn't even know it. I thought being smart was a personality trait and not something you actually had to maintain.
And A-levels are the moment the system stops rewarding you for being quick and starts asking if you can actually sit down and do the work.
I could not sit down and do the work.
BBDD hit and everyone knew. That's the thing about public failure when you've been publicly impressive, people do the maths for you.
But I think about it now and that was the first time I learned anything useful.
Everything I've built since, the restaurant, the agency career, Draper, came from a version of me that got humbled at 17 and finally figured out that showing up when it's boring is the entire game.
It's results day today. If your numbers aren't what you expected I'm not going to give you the rejection is redirection speech.
I'll just say BBDD was probably the best thing that happened to me tbh.

item.title: The best thing I did at Goldman Sachs was talk my way onto someone else's janky side proje…
item.description:
The best thing I did at Goldman Sachs was talk my way onto someone else's janky side project.
Mehti prayed next to me every day.
One afternoon on the way out I asked how it was going. I meant it as a greeting. He heard it as a question about his startup, and started telling me everything.
He'd coded it himself and it barely worked. The idea was that every like turns into a penny for charity, so content creators could fundraise just by posting.
I couldn't stop thinking about it.
So I asked if I could work on it.
I was 19. The whole company was two co-founders, one engineer, and me.
We got into an accelerator called Fast Forward in Stratford. My Goldman apprenticeship was three days work, two days uni, so I started skipping the uni days and going to the programme instead.
I didn't have a growth strategy. I just started posting about what we were building on Twitter because it felt like the obvious thing to do.
Then I found a hook that made people finally get what MiniDeed was, and one tweet went viral.
That turned into a funnel into a Telegram community, and it kept growing on its own.
Then Ramadan hit.
High profile Muslim creators started reaching out, New Arab, Islam Channel. We ran a campaign and the numbers got kind of mad. 26,000 donations, 800,000 taps, 47,000 posts across 26 countries.
oh btw - he never did tell me how he was doing.
